claim: SIMR-1 localizes to perinuclear foci adjacent to or colocalizing with MUT-16 foci.
source: Live imaging of SIMR-1::mCherry demonstrate that it is adjacent to or colocalizes with MUT-16::GFP foci.
evidence: Figure 1B shows live imaging demonstrating the localization pattern.

claim: SIMR-1 is related to C. japonica CJA21107, C. brenneri CBN15556, C. remanei CRE08315, and C. elegans HPO-40.
source: Cladogram representing the relationship between SIMR-1 and related proteins CJA21107 (C. japonica), CBN15556 (C. brenneri), CRE08315 (C. remanei), and HPO-40 (C. elegans).
evidence: Figure 1C shows a cladogram generated from protein alignment.

claim: mut-16 is not required for SIMR-1 foci formation.
source: Live imaging of SIMR-1::mCherry in a mut-16 mutant and MUT-16::GFP in a simr-1; hpo-40 double mutant indicate that mut-16 is not required for SIMR-1 foci formation, nor are simr-1 and hpo-40 required for Mutator foci formation.
evidence: Figure 1D shows live imaging demonstrating independent localization.

claim: simr-1 and hpo-40 are not required for Mutator foci formation.
source: Live imaging of SIMR-1::mCherry in a mut-16 mutant and MUT-16::GFP in a simr-1; hpo-40 double mutant indicate that mut-16 is not required for SIMR-1 foci formation, nor are simr-1 and hpo-40 required for Mutator foci formation.
evidence: Figure 1D shows live imaging demonstrating independent localization.

claim: SIMR-1 contains an extended Tudor domain with four aromatic residues that form an aromatic cage.
source: The four aromatic residues that constitute the aromatic cage are highlighted in blue and the absolutely conserved arginine and aspartate residues characteristic of extended Tudor domains are highlighted in red.
evidence: Figure 1E shows protein alignment highlighting conserved residues.

claim: SIMR-1 is missing two of the four aromatic residues that form the aromatic cage in canonical Tudor domains.
source: SIMR-1 is missing two of these four aromatic residues, making it unclear whether it is functional to recognize a methylated substrate (Figure 1E).
evidence: The text describes the structural analysis of SIMR-1's Tudor domain.

claim: The simr-1[R159C] mutation is located in the Tudor domain.
source: The location of the simr-1[R159C] mutation is marked with an asterisk.
evidence: Figure 1E shows the location of the mutation in the protein alignment.

claim: RSD-2 localizes to perinuclear foci adjacent to or colocalizing with MUT-16 foci.
source: Live imaging of RSD-2::mCherry (C) and HPO-40::mCherry (D) demonstrates that both proteins are adjacent to or colocalize with MUT-16::GFP foci.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows live imaging demonstrating the localization pattern.

claim: HPO-40 localizes to perinuclear foci adjacent to or colocalizing with MUT-16 foci.
source: Live imaging of RSD-2::mCherry (C) and HPO-40::mCherry (D) demonstrates that both proteins are adjacent to or colocalize with MUT-16::GFP foci.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows live imaging demonstrating the localization pattern.

claim: C33G3.6 shows no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels.
source: Two of the uncharacterized proteins, MATH-33 and Y57G11C.3 localize to the nucleus of germ cells and three more, F37C4.5, HGO-1, and C33G3.6, showed no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes localization analysis results.

claim: F37C4.5 shows no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels.
source: Two of the uncharacterized proteins, MATH-33 and Y57G11C.3 localize to the nucleus of germ cells and three more, F37C4.5, HGO-1, and C33G3.6, showed no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes localization analysis results.

claim: HGO-1 shows no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels.
source: Two of the uncharacterized proteins, MATH-33 and Y57G11C.3 localize to the nucleus of germ cells and three more, F37C4.5, HGO-1, and C33G3.6, showed no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes localization analysis results.

claim: MATH-33 localizes to the nucleus of germ cells.
source: Two of the uncharacterized proteins, MATH-33 and Y57G11C.3 localize to the nucleus of germ cells and three more, F37C4.5, HGO-1, and C33G3.6, showed no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes localization analysis results.

claim: Y57G11C.3 localizes to the nucleus of germ cells.
source: Two of the uncharacterized proteins, MATH-33 and Y57G11C.3 localize to the nucleus of germ cells and three more, F37C4.5, HGO-1, and C33G3.6, showed no obvious fluorescence in the cytoplasm or nucleus of germ cells above background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes localization analysis results.

claim: simr-1 mutants are not defective in somatic RNAi.
source: All deletions, including simr-1, elicited RNAi phenotypes similar to wild-type animals indicating that these genes are not required for exogenous RNAi (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows RNAi assay results.

claim: simr-1 mutants are not defective in germline RNAi.
source: All deletions, including simr-1, elicited RNAi phenotypes similar to wild-type animals indicating that these genes are not required for exogenous RNAi (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows RNAi assay results.

claim: hpo-40 single mutants are not defective in exogenous RNAi.
source: Both the single and double mutants elicited RNAi phenotypes similar to wild-type animals indicating that neither hpo-40 alone nor the two proteins acting together are required for exogenous RNAi (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows RNAi assay results.

claim: simr-1; hpo-40 double mutants are not defective in exogenous RNAi.
source: Both the single and double mutants elicited RNAi phenotypes similar to wild-type animals indicating that neither hpo-40 alone nor the two proteins acting together are required for exogenous RNAi (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows RNAi assay results.

claim: simr-1 mutants have reduced small RNAs mapping to mutator-target genes.
source: We observed a substantial reduction in total small RNAs mapping to these mutator-target genes when known components of the mutator complex or RNA silencing pathway, such as mut-16, wago-1, rde-8, or nyn-1; nyn-2 are disrupted (Figure 2C). We also observed a reduction in small RNAs mapping to the mutator-target genes, albeit more modest, in math-33 and simr-1 mutants (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Figure 2C-D shows small RNA sequencing data.

claim: simr-1 mutants have no change in small RNAs mapping to CSR-1-target genes.
source: In contrast to the mutator-target genes, we observed no change in total small RNAs mapping to CSR-1-target genes in the simr-1 mutant (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows small RNA sequencing data.

claim: hpo-40 single mutants have no significant reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs.
source: We observed no significant reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs in the hpo-40 single mutant, and the reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs in the simr-1; hpo-40 double mutant resembled that of the simr-1 single mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B shows small RNA sequencing data.

claim: simr-1; hpo-40 double mutants have a reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs similar to simr-1 single mutants.
source: We observed no significant reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs in the hpo-40 single mutant, and the reduction in mutator-dependent small RNAs in the simr-1; hpo-40 double mutant resembled that of the simr-1 single mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B shows small RNA sequencing data.

claim: simr-1 mutants have a mortal germline phenotype at 25°C.
source: In contrast, wild-type animals displayed a 40.3% reduction in brood size and simr-1 mutants displayed a 59.0% reduction in brood size after a single generation at 25°C compared to 20°C (Figure 3A). However, unlike wild-type animals which remained fertile after more than 11 generations at 25°C, simr-1 mutants became progressively sterile over the next 10 generations at 25°C until reaching complete sterility at generation 11 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows brood size data across generations at 25°C.

claim: mut-16 mutants are sterile after one generation at 25°C.
source: mut-16 mutants were included as a control and, as expected, fertility was reduced by 95.3% in the first generation at 25°C, with the few fertile animals producing only sterile progeny by the second generation at 25°C (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows brood size data for mut-16 mutants.

claim: The fertility of simr-1 mutants recovers after returning to 20°C from 25°C.
source: To address this possibility, we selected wild-type and simr-1 mutant animals raised for 10 generations at 25°C, and returned them to 20°C. Within approximately four generations at 20°C, the fertility of simr-1 mutants recovered to within 72.8% of pre-25°C levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows brood size data after temperature shift back to 20°C.

claim: The reduction in simr-1 fertility at 25°C is not primarily due to the accumulation of DNA mutations.
source: These data indicate that the reduction in simr-1 fertility at 25°C is not primarily due to the accumulation of DNA mutations, but may be due to transcriptional or chromatin changes that can be reset after recovery at 20°C, similar to what has been observed previously for hrde-1 and hrde-2 (Spracklin et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: The inference is based on the recovery of fertility after temperature shift.

claim: simr-1 mutant males raised for 10 generations at 25°C are nearly sterile.
source: simr-1 mutant males raised for a single generation at 25°C sired fewer progeny than the wild-type control males, and simr-1 mutant males raised for 10 generations at 25°C were nearly sterile, similar to simr-1 hermaphrodites raised for 10 generations at 25°C (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows mating assay data.

claim: simr-1 mutant hermaphrodites raised for 10 generations at 25°C are nearly sterile even when provided with wild-type sperm.
source: In contrast, after 10 generations at 25°C, simr-1 mutant hermaphrodites were nearly sterile, even when provided with wild-type sperm (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows mating assay data.

claim: Both spermatogenesis and oogenesis are defective in simr-1 mutants raised at elevated temperature for multiple generations.
source: These data indicate that both spermatogenesis and oogenesis are defective in simr-1 mutants raised at elevated temperature for multiple generations.
evidence: The conclusion is based on mating assays shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: simr-1 mutants have increased germ cell apoptosis after 10 or 11 generations at 25°C compared to wild-type.
source: However, only after 10 or 11 generations at 25°C does the number of apoptotic germ cells in simr-1 mutants rise significantly compared to wild-type animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: Figure 3E shows apoptotic cell counts.

claim: simr-1[A11V] and simr-1[R159C] alleles desilence the piRNA sensor in a henn-1 mutant background.
source: From this screen we identified two alleles of simr-1 that further desilence the piRNA sensor transgene in the henn-1 mutant background (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows images of GFP expression from the piRNA sensor.

claim: simr-1 deletion mutant is not sufficient to desilence the piRNA sensor transgene in the absence of the henn-1 mutant.
source: Interestingly, when we crossed our simr-1 deletion mutant into the piRNA sensor strain without the henn-1 mutant, we observed that simr-1 was not sufficient to desilence the piRNA sensor transgene in the absence of the henn-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), similar to what has been observed previously with prg-1 (Luteijn et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows images of the piRNA sensor.

claim: mut-16 mutants robustly desilence the piRNA sensor transgene.
source: In contrast, a mutation in mut-16 robustly desilences the same piRNA sensor transgene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows images of the piRNA sensor.

claim: simr-1 mutants cannot desilence the ERGO-1-dependent 22G-siR1 sensor.
source: A mutation in simr-1 was unable to desilence the 22G-siR1 sensor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows images of the 22G-siR1 sensor.

claim: mut-16 mutants robustly desilence the 22G-siR1 sensor.
source: In contrast, a mutation in mut-16 robustly desilenced the 22G-siR1 sensor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows images of the 22G-siR1 sensor.

claim: simr-1 mutants do not display an Enhanced RNAi (Eri) phenotype.
source: Furthermore, when animals with mutations in the ERGO-1 26G-siRNA pathway, like eri-7 (Fischer et al., 2008), are fed lir-1, hmr-1, or dpy-13 double-strand RNA, they display an Enhanced RNAi (Eri) phenotype which was not observed with the simr-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows RNAi assay results.

claim: SIMR-1 is required to prevent sterility after reestablishing WAGO-class 22G-siRNA production.
source: In fact, this result is what we observed. In the control cross (mut-14 smut-1 males mated to mut-7 unc-119 hermaphrodites), only 13.0% of the F1 heterozygous progeny were sterile (Figure 4B). In contrast, when the simr-1 mutation is present in both parental strains (simr-1; mut-14 smut-1 males mated to simr-1; mut-7 unc-119 hermaphrodites) the percentage of sterile progeny increased to 47.1%, and for the prg-1 cross (prg-1; mut-14 smut-1 males mated to prg-1; mut-7 unc-119 hermaphrodites), the number of sterile animals increases further to 98.8% (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows mating assay results.

claim: The extended Tudor domain is essential for SIMR-1 localization to germline foci.
source: By live imaging, we observed that SIMR-1[R159C]::GFP no longer forms germline foci, despite its clear expression in the cytoplasm of germ cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows live imaging of SIMR-1[R159C]::GFP.

claim: SIMR-1[R159C]::GFP is expressed at wild-type levels.
source: We further confirmed that SIMR-1[R159C]::GFP is expressed at wild-type levels by western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1D shows western blot data.

claim: simr-1[R159C]::gfp exhibits progressive sterility at elevated temperature similar to the simr-1 deletion allele.
source: Like the simr-1 deletion allele, simr-1[R159C]::gfp exhibited progressive sterility at elevated temperature, becoming sterile after approximately 10–11 generations (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows brood size data across generations.

claim: The extended Tudor domain is essential for SIMR-1 function.
source: Together, these data show that the extended Tudor domain is essential for SIMR-1 function, and that disruption of the Tudor domain results in loss of SIMR-1 germline foci and causes a Mrt phenotype similar to that of the simr-1 deletion allele.
evidence: The conclusion is based on localization and fertility data for simr-1[R159C].

claim: 817 genes were depleted of small RNAs in simr-1 mutants at 20°C compared to wild-type.
source: In simr-1 mutants, 817 genes were depleted of small RNAs and 213 genes were enriched for small RNAs at 20°C when compared to wild-type at 20°C (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Figure 5A shows a table of genes with changed small RNA levels.

claim: 213 genes were enriched for small RNAs in simr-1 mutants at 20°C compared to wild-type.
source: In simr-1 mutants, 817 genes were depleted of small RNAs and 213 genes were enriched for small RNAs at 20°C when compared to wild-type at 20°C (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Figure 5A shows a table of genes with changed small RNA levels.

claim: 1258 genes were depleted of small RNAs in simr-1 mutants after one generation at 25°C compared to wild-type.
source: After one generation at 25°C, 1258 genes were depleted of small RNAs and 2712 genes were enriched for small RNAs compared to wild-type also cultured for one generation at 25°C (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Figure 5A shows a table of genes with changed small RNA levels.

claim: 2712 genes were enriched for small RNAs in simr-1 mutants after one generation at 25°C compared to wild-type.
source: After one generation at 25°C, 1258 genes were depleted of small RNAs and 2712 genes were enriched for small RNAs compared to wild-type also cultured for one generation at 25°C (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Figure 5A shows a table of genes with changed small RNA levels.

claim: Small RNAs from mutator-target genes are reduced in simr-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: In contrast, small RNAs from mutator-target genes and piRNA-target genes were reduced in simr-1 mutants at both 20°C and 25°C (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5B-C shows box plots and heat maps of small RNA levels.

claim: Small RNAs from piRNA-target genes are reduced in simr-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: In contrast, small RNAs from mutator-target genes and piRNA-target genes were reduced in simr-1 mutants at both 20°C and 25°C (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5B-C shows box plots and heat maps of small RNA levels.

claim: Small RNAs from CSR-1-target genes are up-regulated in simr-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: Small RNAs derived from CSR-1-target genes were modestly up-regulated at 20°C and more dramatically up-regulated after a single generation 25°C in simr-1 mutants (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5B-C shows box plots and heat maps of small RNA levels.

claim: 84% of genes with reduced small RNAs in simr-1 mutants at 20°C also have reduced small RNAs in prg-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: 84% of genes with reduced small RNAs in a simr-1 mutant at 20°C also have reduced small RNAs in a prg-1 mutant at 20°C (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows a Venn diagram of overlapping genes.

claim: SIMR-1 is not required for piRNA biogenesis or stability.
source: Similarly to what has been previously reported, piRNA expression is significantly reduced at 25°C compared to 20°C in wild-type animals (Belicard et al., 2018). However, we observed no significant difference between total piRNA levels in simr-1 mutants compared to wild-type animals at either temperature (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows piRNA levels in wild-type and simr-1 mutants.

claim: Less than 1% of piRNAs are reduced by at least two-fold in simr-1 mutants.
source: In contrast to prg-1 mutants in which 83% of piRNAs are reduced by at least two-fold, in simr-1 mutants less than 1% of piRNAs are reduced by at least two-fold (Figure 5F).
evidence: Figure 5F shows scatter plots of piRNA levels.

claim: SIMR-1 functions downstream of piRNA biogenesis.
source: These data together indicate that SIMR-1 functions downstream of piRNA biogenesis.
evidence: The conclusion is based on piRNA levels being unaffected in simr-1 mutants.

claim: Small RNAs mapping to Tc2 are significantly reduced in simr-1 mutants at 20°C and 25°C.
source: Small RNAs mapping to Tc2 and Tc3 were significantly reduced in both the simr-1 mutant as well as in a mut-16 mutant, at both 20°C and 25°C (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 6A shows small RNA levels mapping to transposons.

claim: Small RNAs mapping to Tc3 are significantly reduced in simr-1 mutants at 20°C and 25°C.
source: Small RNAs mapping to Tc2 and Tc3 were significantly reduced in both the simr-1 mutant as well as in a mut-16 mutant, at both 20°C and 25°C (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 6A shows small RNA levels mapping to transposons.

claim: Small RNAs mapping to Tc1 are not reduced in simr-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, small RNAs mapping to Tc1 and Tc4v, the variant of Tc4 containing the Tc4 transposase mRNA sequence (Li and Shaw, 1993), were not reduced in simr-1 mutants (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 6A shows small RNA levels mapping to transposons.

claim: Small RNAs mapping to Tc4v are not reduced in simr-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, small RNAs mapping to Tc1 and Tc4v, the variant of Tc4 containing the Tc4 transposase mRNA sequence (Li and Shaw, 1993), were not reduced in simr-1 mutants (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 6A shows small RNA levels mapping to transposons.

claim: SIMR-1 is required for small RNA production at piRNA-targeted transposons but not at transposons targeted independently of piRNAs.
source: These data indicate that SIMR-1 is required for small RNA production or maintenance at piRNA-targeted transposons but not at transposons targeted independently of piRNAs.
evidence: The conclusion is based on differential effects on Tc2/Tc3 vs Tc1/Tc4v.

claim: 28 histone genes are enriched for small RNAs in both simr-1 and prg-1 mutants.
source: Of the 104 genes enriched for small RNAs in both simr-1 and prg-1 mutants, 28 are histone genes (Figure 6C; Pettitt et al., 2002).
evidence: Figure 6C shows a Venn diagram and pie chart of histone genes.

claim: Histone genes are highly enriched for small RNAs in both simr-1 and prg-1 mutants.
source: Overall, histone genes are highly enriched for small RNAs in both simr-1 and prg-1 mutants, though this enrichment is lessened across multiple generations at 25°C, suggesting that it may not be associated with the sterility phenotype (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows box plots of small RNA levels at histone genes.

claim: The majority of histone genes are unchanged or depleted of small RNAs in mut-16 mutants.
source: Nonetheless, this enrichment of small RNAs at histone genes in both simr-1 and prg-1 mutants is clearly in contrast to mut-16 mutants at 20°C and 25°C, where the majority of histone genes are unchanged or depleted of small RNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows box plots of small RNA levels at histone genes.

claim: 139 genes have reduced mRNA expression in simr-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: We identified 139 genes whose mRNA expression was reduced by at least two-fold in simr-1 mutants at 20°C and 164 genes whose mRNA expression was increased by at least two-fold in simr-1 mutants at 20°C (Figure 6F and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Figure 6F shows a table of genes with changed mRNA expression.

claim: 164 genes have increased mRNA expression in simr-1 mutants at 20°C.
source: We identified 139 genes whose mRNA expression was reduced by at least two-fold in simr-1 mutants at 20°C and 164 genes whose mRNA expression was increased by at least two-fold in simr-1 mutants at 20°C (Figure 6F and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Figure 6F shows a table of genes with changed mRNA expression.

claim: The majority of SIMR-1-target genes are not derepressed in a simr-1 mutant.
source: These data indicate that the majority of SIMR-1-target genes are not derepressed in a simr-1 mutant, which suggests that either SIMR-1-dependent siRNAs are required only to initiate but not maintain silencing of their targets or that additional layers of regulation maintain silencing of these genes in the absence of SIMR-1-dependent siRNAs.
evidence: The conclusion is based on the lack of correlation between small RNA loss and mRNA increase.

claim: Histone genes have reduced mRNA expression in simr-1 mutants.
source: Histone genes, including H2A and H3, were amongst those genes enriched for small RNAs and with reduced mRNA expression in simr-1 mutants (Figure 6D–E and I, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), similar to what has previously been observed in prg-1 mutants (Barucci et al., 2020; Reed et al., 2020).
evidence: Figure 6I shows box plots of histone mRNA expression.

claim: SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with Mutator foci but do not fully colocalize.
source: We observed that SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with Mutator foci (96.4% of the time with no empty space between fluorescent signals, n = 56 SIMR-1 foci), however they do not fully colocalize suggesting that they are distinct structures (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 7A shows immunostaining images.

claim: SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with P granules but do not fully colocalize.
source: SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with both P granules and with Z granules (100% of the time with P granules, n = 56 SIMR-1 foci, and 100% of the time with Z granules, n = 62 SIMR-1 foci). However, we found that SIMR-1 foci do not fully colocalize with either structure, and in some cases multiple SIMR-1 foci can associate with a single focus of another granule type (Figure 7A, see inset for SIMR-1 and ZNFX-1 localization).
evidence: Figure 7A shows immunostaining images.

claim: SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with Z granules but do not fully colocalize.
source: SIMR-1 foci are closely associated with both P granules and with Z granules (100% of the time with P granules, n = 56 SIMR-1 foci, and 100% of the time with Z granules, n = 62 SIMR-1 foci). However, we found that SIMR-1 foci do not fully colocalize with either structure, and in some cases multiple SIMR-1 foci can associate with a single focus of another granule type (Figure 7A, see inset for SIMR-1 and ZNFX-1 localization).
evidence: Figure 7A shows immunostaining images.

claim: SIMR-1 foci are more closely associated with Z granules than with P granules.
source: SIMR-1 foci do appear to be more closely associated with Z granules than with P granules and quantification of distances between fluorescence centers of each foci supports this observation (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows quantification of distances between foci.

claim: SIMR-1 is not required for PRG-1 localization or expression.
source: Furthermore, SIMR-1 is not required for PRG-1 localization or expression, and PRG-1 is not required for SIMR-1 localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C shows live imaging and western blot data.

claim: PRG-1 is not required for SIMR-1 localization.
source: Furthermore, SIMR-1 is not required for PRG-1 localization or expression, and PRG-1 is not required for SIMR-1 localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C shows live imaging and western blot data.

claim: SIMR-1 and RSD-2 are highly coincident, suggesting they may localize to the same perinuclear structure.
source: Following immunostaining, we observed that SIMR-1 and RSD-2 were highly coincident, suggesting SIMR-1 and RSD-2 may localize to the same perinuclear structure (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Figure 7A-B shows immunostaining images and distance quantification.

claim: ZNFX-1 localizes between SIMR-1 and PGL-1 in a stacked arrangement.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the foci appeared to be stacked, with ZNFX-1 localizing between SIMR-1 and PGL-1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows immunostaining images of three proteins.

claim: There are at least four separate compartments at the nuclear periphery in C. elegans germ cells that constitute C. elegans nuage.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that there are at least four separate compartments at the nuclear periphery in C. elegans germ cells, that together constitute C. elegans nuage, each with unique protein components and a distinct molecular role in the RNA silencing pathway.
evidence: The conclusion is based on localization data showing distinct but adjacent compartments.

claim: SIMR-1 acts downstream of piRNA production and upstream of mutator complex-dependent siRNA biogenesis.
source: Here, we identify the Tudor domain protein, SIMR-1, as acting downstream of piRNA production and upstream of mutator complex-dependent siRNA biogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: SIMR-1 localizes to distinct subcellular foci adjacent to P granules and Mutator foci.
source: Interestingly, SIMR-1 also localizes to distinct subcellular foci adjacent to P granules and Mutator foci, two phase-separated condensates that are the sites of piRNA-dependent mRNA recognition and mutator complex-dependent siRNA amplification, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Multiple perinuclear condensates organize the piRNA pathway and promote mRNA regulation by the mutator complex.
source: Thus, our data suggests a role for multiple perinuclear condensates in organizing the piRNA pathway and promoting mRNA regulation by the mutator complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: piRNAs play a critical role in the regulation of transposons and other germline genes.
source: piRNAs play a critical role in the regulation of transposons and other germline genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as background knowledge.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, regulation of piRNA target genes is mediated by the mutator complex, which synthesizes high levels of siRNAs through the activity of an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, regulation of piRNA target genes is mediated by the mutator complex, which synthesizes high levels of siRNAs through the activity of an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as background knowledge.

claim: The steps between mRNA recognition by the piRNA pathway and siRNA amplification by the mutator complex are unknown.
source: However, the steps between mRNA recognition by the piRNA pathway and siRNA amplification by the mutator complex are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Argonaute proteins are key mediators of RNA silencing.
source: Argonaute proteins are key mediators of RNA silencing; by binding to small RNAs, which interact with fully or partially complementary mRNAs, the Argonaute proteins can promote transcription repression, translation inhibition, and RNA decay of targeted mRNAs (Hutvagner and Simard, 2008; Claycomb, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: piRNAs are bound by Piwi proteins.
source: piRNAs are bound by a subgroup of Argonaute proteins called Piwi proteins, of which C. elegans has a single functional homolog, PRG-1 (Batista et al., 2008; Das et al., 2008; Wang and Reinke, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: C. elegans has a single functional Piwi protein homolog, PRG-1.
source: piRNAs are bound by a subgroup of Argonaute proteins called Piwi proteins, of which C. elegans has a single functional homolog, PRG-1 (Batista et al., 2008; Das et al., 2008; Wang and Reinke, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The ping-pong mechanism amplifies piRNAs in many organisms but is not found in nematodes.
source: In many organisms, including mammals, flies, and zebrafish, piRNAs are amplified through the ping-pong mechanism (Brennecke et al., 2007; Aravin et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007; Houwing et al., 2007). This mechanism, however, is not found in nematodes.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: C. elegans employs a mutator complex-dependent small RNA amplification pathway to reinforce silencing at piRNA target loci.
source: Rather, C. elegans employs a different mechanism to reinforce silencing at piRNA target loci. In C. elegans, a small RNA amplification pathway dependent on the mutator complex, which includes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, synthesizes secondary downstream siRNAs from piRNA-targeted mRNAs to trigger robust and heritable silencing (Das et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2012; Bagijn et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012; Ashe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: WAGO-class 22G-siRNAs are approximately 22-nt long, often start with a 5'G, and are bound by the WAGO clade of Argonaute proteins.
source: These siRNAs are approximately 22-nt long, often start with a 5'G, and are bound by the WAGO clade of Argonaute proteins, including WAGO-1, therefore, they are often referred to as WAGO-class 22G-siRNAs (Pak and Fire, 2007; Sijen et al., 2007; Yigit et al., 2006; Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Tudor domain proteins in many organisms play critical roles in piRNA accumulation and mRNA target regulation through their interaction with PIWI proteins.
source: Tudor domain proteins in many organisms, including both mouse and Drosophila, play critical roles in piRNA accumulation and mRNA target regulation through their interaction with PIWI proteins (Reuter et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2011; Nishida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Tudor domains recognize methylated arginines or lysines and can mediate protein interactions in a methylation-specific manner.
source: Tudor domains, which function as protein-protein interaction modules, recognize methylated arginines or lysines and thus can mediate protein interactions in a methylation-specific manner (Friesen et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The extended Tudor domain preferentially recognizes symmetrically dimethylated arginine (sDMA) modifications.
source: The extended Tudor domain preferentially recognizes symmetrically dimethylated arginine (sDMA) modifications over monomethylated arginines (MMA), asymmetrically dimethylated arginines (aDMA), or unmodified peptides; however, some extended Tudor domain proteins have lost the ability to bind the methylated arginine mark and recognize only unmodified peptides (Liu et al., 2010b; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: P granules assemble by intracellular phase separation.
source: Seminal work in C. elegans has shown that P granules assemble by intracellular phase separation (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: Mutator foci and Z granules are phase-separated biomolecular condensates adjacent to P granules.
source: More recently, both Mutator foci, the sites of secondary siRNA biogenesis by the mutator complex, and Z granules, which are required for RNAi inheritance, have been shown to be phase-separated biomolecular condensates which lie adjacent to one another and the P granule at the nuclear periphery (Uebel et al., 2018; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: MUT-16 is a scaffolding protein required for assembly of the mutator complex.
source: Because MUT-16 is a scaffolding protein required for assembly of the mutator complex (Phillips et al., 2012), we chose to use an endogenously tagged MUT-16::GFP::3xFLAG for immunoprecipitation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results with a citation.

claim: The IP-mass spec experiment identified 17 candidate MUT-16 interactors, twelve of which comprise all known members of the mutator complex.
source: In total, we identified 17 candidate MUT-16 interactors, twelve of which comprise all known members of the mutator complex (Phillips et al., 2012; Uebel et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2015) and five previously uncharacterized proteins (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citations.

claim: RSD-2 is a small RNA factor required for exogenous RNAi introduced at low doses.
source: RSD-2 is a small RNA factor required for exogenous RNAi introduced at low doses and not previously known to interact with the mutator complex (Sakaguchi et al., 2014; Han et al., 2008; Tijsterman et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citations.

claim: WAGO-1 is an Argonaute protein that localizes to P granules.
source: WAGO-1 is an Argonaute protein that localizes to P granules but was found to interact with MUT-16 in a yeast two-hybrid screen (Supplementary file 1; Gu et al., 2009; Phillips et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citations.

claim: MATH-33 is a ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase previously identified in a proteomics screen of RDE-10-interacting proteins.
source: MATH-33 is a ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase that was previously identified in a proteomics screen of RDE-10-interacting proteins and RNAi screen for genes involved in co-suppression, a phenomenon where repetitive transgenes silence homologous endogenous genes (Zhang et al., 2012; Robert et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citations.
